hints: Focus on counting total electrons first, remembering that a positive charge means electrons have been lost.
Add up the electrons for N plus four H atoms, then subtract one for the 1+ charge to get 10 electrons.
Look for the neutral atom whose atomic number equals that electron count, since atoms have equal protons and electrons.
walkthrough:
**Count the electrons in the ammonium ion**

Think of $\text{NH}_4^+$ as one nitrogen joined to four hydrogens, with an overall 1+ charge.

Electrons if neutral: $7 + (4 \times 1) = 11$

**Adjust for the positive charge**

A 1+ charge means one electron has been lost compared to the neutral atoms.

$$\text{electrons in } \text{NH}_4^+ = 11 - 1 = 10$$

**Find the atom with 10 electrons**

A neutral atom has electrons = protons = atomic number. So we need atomic number 10.

$$\text{Ne has atomic number 10, so Ne has 10 electrons}$$

options.A: Mg has atomic number 12, so a neutral Mg atom has 12 electrons. That is 2 too many, so it does not match the 10 electrons in ammonium.
options.B: Na has atomic number 11, so a neutral Na atom has 11 electrons. Students often forget to subtract one electron for the 1+ charge on ammonium and pick this trap.
options.C: Ne has atomic number 10, so a neutral Ne atom has 10 electrons. This exactly matches the 10 electrons in $\text{NH}_4^+$, so they are isoelectronic.
options.D: O has atomic number 8, so a neutral O atom has 8 electrons. That is 2 too few, so it does not match the ammonium ion.
